title: A Proven Way to Keep Teachers in Needy Schools is Losing Ground

content: This article was originally published in Chalkbeat. States and school districts all across the country face the same problem: Teachers are far more likely to leave high-poverty schools, creating constant churn that hurts students from low-income families. This pattern shows up literally everywhere I can find data: Alaska , Florida , Missouri , New York City , Pennsylvania , South Carolina , Virginia , Wisconsin , and Washington state. Many challenges in education are hard to understand and difficult to solve. This is not one of them. Educators are more likely to leave disadvantaged schools because they’re more challenging to teach in. Extra pay for teachers in those schools can help address this problem and create a more stable workforce. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter But only 12 states have such pay incentives, according to a recent analysis by the National Council on Teacher Quality. The number has actually declined in recent years. “States [are] ignoring this as a possible policy lever to improve teacher effectiveness and to attract and retain more great teachers where we really need them,” says Heather Peske, president of NCTQ. This problem is long-standing. In Missouri, for instance, in every single year since at least 2009, far more teachers left the state’s highest-poverty schools, often at twice the rate of more affluent ones. Or consider New York City, the country’s largest school system, which is highly stratified by economic need. The city’s most disadvantaged schools lost nearly 1 in 6 teachers in 2024; better-off schools lost just 1 in 12. In high-poverty schools, constant and cumulative churn means more inexperienced teachers who struggle to manage a classroom. For administrators, all the turnover means it’s difficult to sustain new initiatives or a strong school culture. In recent years, more teachers have left the classroom overall, exacerbating existing challenges in high-needs schools. Fortunately, there is a solution: extra pay. A Dallas program, for instance, paid teachers between $8,000 and $14,000 (adjusted for inflation) to work in struggling schools. This helped bring in more experienced and effective teachers, researchers found . Alongside a series of other reforms, student achievement rose substantially. Once the extra pay ended, though, teacher turnover rose and test scores fell. Studies in North Carolina , Florida , San Francisco , Tennessee , Texas , and Washington have also found that pay bumps or bonuses make the school more appealing for outside applicants or help keep existing teachers. “We do see pretty clearly that they work,” says Christopher Redding, a University of Florida education professor who has studied teacher turnover in the state. As the NCTQ report shows, however, such salary incentives remain rare at the state level. Even when they do exist, the extra pay is typically too small to fully close turnover gaps between needy and advantaged schools. So why is this research-supported idea so uncommon? Well, extra pay for educators in high-needs schools costs money and is competing against a bevy of other priorities. And there is no strong political constituency for this. Parents in those schools do not have lobbyists, and school district leaders may prefer to get extra money directly, which often does not translate into higher teacher pay. When salary incentives are put in place, they may be cut in tight budget times. Politically influential teachers unions have been skeptical of pay incentives. “Bonuses for teaching certain subjects or working in hard-to-staff schools may help attract educators, but they are not a substitute for addressing the underlying challenges facing public education: inadequate resources, support, and working conditions,” National Education Association President Princess Moss said in a statement. “Our goal should be to make every school a place where educators want to work.” A spokesperson for the American Federation of Teachers, the country’s other large educator union, said AFT is open to salary incentives, pointing to the union contract in Philadelphia. It allows the district to pay bonuses of up to $5,000 for teachers in certain hard-to-staff schools. Arthur Steinberg, the head of the Philadelphia union, told me this idea came from management as a way to stabilize schools that were constantly losing teachers. It’s not the approach the union would have preferred. “All of our teachers are underpaid, so our initial reaction was: Pay everybody,” he said. The union accepted the incentives as part of the give and take in negotiation. “We were able to secure some other wins in exchange for this,” Steinberg said. He declined to say whether the union would back this measure in future contract negotiations. States with weaker teachers unions are more likely to have pay incentives for high-poverty schools, though plenty of states with weak unions don’t. It is more common for large school districts to offer such incentives but they tend to be small in size and have limited reach. Much of the turnover gap is about differences across districts — Philadelphia versus its more advantaged suburbs, for instance — rather than within a single district. To step back, the reason why these large teacher turnover gaps exist is because low- and high-income students often don’t go to school together.Policymakers could address this through economic integration, effectively limiting the number of highly disadvantaged schools where teachers are reluctant to work. Or they could make sure any disadvantaged schools are staffed by relatively stable teacher workforces using the proven lever of teacher pay bumps. If policymakers don’t pursue either option, no one should be surprised by the consequences. This story was originally published by Chalkbeat, a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters .

title: Texas Sports Academy, Tied to AI-Driven Alpha School, is Texas’ Biggest Voucher Recipient So Far

content: This article was originally published in The Texas Tribune. The biggest recipient of Texas’ new school voucher program so far is a sports academy connected to Alpha School, the artificial intelligence-driven private school chain that the state’s education board rejected for a charter school last year. Texas Sports Academy, which calls itself an “elite sports academy built for serious student-athletes,” had received $6.5 million in voucher dollars as of Oct. 30, according to the Texas Comptroller’s online dashboard . That’s more than twice the amount received by the second-largest recipient, San Antonio-based Cornerstone Christian Schools, which had gotten roughly $2.8 million. The disclosure comes a little more than a year after the State Board of Education voted 10-3 to reject Alpha leaders’ bid to open a publicly funded charter school. Board members raised concerns about the company’s use of AI to teach, about students’ screen time and about the large test-score gains Alpha leaders presented. Texas Sports Academy, which has several schools across the state in addition to a virtual campus, is one of numerous institutions across the country connected to Alpha. Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter But Alpha’s rejection by the SBOE did not prevent it from participating in the voucher program, which allows families to receive state funding for use at private schools and for home schooling. As of September, the chain had roughly quadrupled its Texas private schools in the state to more than 30 virtual and in-person campuses, and most were accepted into the voucher program, an investigation by The Texas Tribune and ProPublica found . Alpha’s model has students complete core academics online in two hours a day using AI software, a tool the state’s education commissioner, Mike Morath, and his agency have helped get into at least three public school districts this year. At Texas Sports Academy, an AI tutor “guides students through each lesson,” according to the school’s website , a setup that it says “leaves the rest of the day free for sports training, developing life skills, pursuing passions, and just being a kid.” Related Inside Alpha School’s ‘Bootcamp’: Heart Monitors, Unpaid Labor & Many, Many Tweets After a couple hours of academics, the rest of the day is filled with various sports classes, such as soccer training, speed and agility training, and strength training, according to a sample student schedule . On Fridays at 3:30 p.m., an hour can be set aside for NBA watch parties. The figures are public on a dashboard that outgoing Texas Comptroller Don Huffines said Friday his office is in the process of expanding. In a news release, Huffines said the expansion is intended to increase “insight into how TEFA funds are being used while maintaining protections for student and family privacy.” TEFA stands for Texas Education Freedom Accounts, the program’s formal name. Other top recipients included First Baptist Academy, which received almost $2 million; Yeshiva Torat Emet, a Jewish school in Houston which received nearly $1.6 million; and The Christian School at Castle Hills which received a little more than $1.5 million. Texas lawmakers, led by Gov. Greg Abbott , approved the voucher program in 2025. It gives families public funds to help pay for their children’s private school tuition, roughly $10,500, and up to $2,000 for home-schooling expenses . The program also covers a wide range of approved educational expenses, like private tutoring and school supplies. The comptroller’s dashboard shows that Amazon was by far the largest private vendor, receiving $12.3 million. The next largest, Rainbow Resource Center, Inc., received $2.3 million. Lexi Churchill contributed to this report. Disclosure: Amazon has been a financial supporter of The Texas Tribune within the past five years.
